Dermatology · published research

Strawberry hemangioma

A 20-infant case series reported regression and improved lesion color, contour, and texture after 830-nm treatment. Without a comparison group, the contribution of light cannot be separated from natural regression.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A 20-infant case series reported regression and improved lesion color, contour, and texture after 830-nm treatment. Without a comparison group, the contribution of light cannot be separated from natural regression.

Summary of the Evidence

One exact-category publication reports an uncontrolled series of 20 infants treated for strawberry hemangioma. It is a single clinical report, not 20 independent studies, and it includes no randomized or contemporaneous untreated group. Other hemangioma records concern different anatomical sites or combine PBM with sclerotherapy, so they do not provide a clean replication for infantile cutaneous lesions.

Human and clinical evidence

Ohshiro and Chen described regression, restoration of normal color and contour, and return toward normal skin texture in the treated infants. The authors reported that full regression was usually achieved within about four years. The paper does not provide a comparison group or modern standardized lesion measurements, so it cannot show how much faster regression was than the natural course (Ohshiro and Chen 1992).

Natural history is especially important for this condition because many infantile hemangiomas involute over time. The report’s favorable observations are clinically descriptive, but without untreated comparison or adjustment for lesion size, site, and severity, they cannot establish that treatment caused the regression or reduced residual changes. The historical series also predates current standard management choices, so it does not compare PBM with observation or modern medical care.

Animal evidence

No animal study directly addressing strawberry hemangioma was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No hemangioma-specific cell or ex-vivo study was identified in this category.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The case series used an 830-nm near-infrared diode laser at 60 mW for five seconds per point. Points were placed around the lesion at a density of one per 10 cm². This is the only directly reported protocol in the category. There is no dose comparison or study showing whether another wavelength, power, or treatment schedule would produce the same observations.

Interpretation

The publication records favorable lesion regression and skin appearance in 20 treated infants. That outcome is worth preserving in the summary, while its cause remains uncertain because spontaneous involution is common and there was no comparison group. The evidence supports a historical treatment observation, not an established effect on regression time or final appearance.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for faster regression or improved skin appearance with 830-nm treatment
Publications and records1 article

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One uncontrolled historical series of 20 infants reported regression and improved color and texture after near-infrared treatment. Infantile hemangiomas can regress naturally, and there was no untreated comparison or standardized measurement. A modern controlled study with lesion-specific tracking and comparison to current care would be required to determine whether light changes the timing or final appearance.
